name: Brachial plexus
summary: The ventral rami of C5–T1 reorganize in the neck and axilla into the brachial plexus so that fibers from each root are redistributed to several nerves: roots form trunks (upper C5–C6, middle C7, lower C8–T1) between the scalene muscles, trunks split into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle, divisions regroup into cords named for their position around the axillary artery (lateral, posterior, medial), and cords give the terminal nerves. The sequence 'roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches' is the key to localizing plexus injuries: upper trunk lesions (Erb) paralyze the shoulder and elbow flexors, lower trunk lesions (Klumpke) the hand, and cord lesions produce recognizable combinations that no single nerve or root explains.

anatomy.location: From the intervertebral foramina of C5–T1 through the interscalene triangle (roots and trunks), over the first rib behind the clavicle (divisions), and around the axillary artery in the axilla (cords) to the terminal branches at the lower border of pectoralis minor.

subdivisions.name: Roots (C5–T1)
subdivisions.note: dorsal scapular nerve (C5), long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), contributions to the phrenic nerve

subdivisions.name: Trunks
subdivisions.note: upper (C5–C6): suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius; middle (C7); lower (C8–T1)

subdivisions.name: Divisions
subdivisions.note: anterior divisions → flexors (lateral and medial cords); posterior divisions → extensors (posterior cord)

subdivisions.name: Lateral cord
subdivisions.note: musculocutaneous nerve, lateral root of the median nerve, lateral pectoral nerve

subdivisions.name: Posterior cord
subdivisions.note: axillary and radial nerves, subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves

subdivisions.name: Medial cord
subdivisions.note: ulnar nerve, medial root of the median nerve, medial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm

function: Motor and sensory supply of the entire upper limb and shoulder girdle, plus sympathetic fibers distributed with the nerves.

bestView.label: cervical cord: the plexus roots emerge at C5–T1 below the MNI volume

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. Ultrasound and MR neurography image the nerve directly; electrodiagnosis localizes the lesion functionally. MR neurography of the plexus shows the trunks and cords as bright fascicular structures on STIR; thickening, enhancement or discontinuity indicate injury, inflammation or infiltration.

pathology.finding: Pseudomeningocele at an avulsed root on cervical MRI or CT myelography; thickened T2-bright trunks in stretch injury.
Enhancing mass infiltrating the lower plexus (Pancoast tumor, breast cancer, painful, Horner) versus diffuse thickening without mass after radiation (painless, myokymia on EMG).
Focal nerve constrictions or T2 hyperintensity in the upper trunk and its branches with denervation edema in shoulder muscles.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MR neurography (STIR, T1+Gd); EMG/NCS to separate root, plexus and nerve

lesionEffects.deficit: Erb–Duchenne palsy: arm hangs adducted, internally rotated, pronated (waiter's tip)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Upper trunk C5–C6: deltoid, biceps, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, brachioradialis

lesionEffects.deficit: Klumpke palsy: claw hand with intrinsic wasting, often with Horner syndrome
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lower trunk C8–T1, T1 sympathetic fibers

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak elbow flexion and forearm pronation with lateral forearm numbness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lateral cord: musculocutaneous and lateral median fibers

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak wrist and finger extension plus deltoid weakness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Posterior cord: radial and axillary nerves

lesionEffects.deficit: Hand intrinsic and finger flexor weakness with medial arm numbness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Medial cord: ulnar and medial median fibers

examination: Test muscles supplied by different nerves from the same root, and by the same nerve from different roots, to separate root, plexus and nerve
Sensory map: dermatomal (root) versus peripheral nerve versus plexus (cord) territories
Look for Horner syndrome, winging of the scapula and paraspinal wasting (root level)
Tinel sign over the supraclavicular fossa
pearls: Preserved paraspinal and serratus anterior function with a plexus pattern places the lesion beyond the roots
A painful, progressive lower plexopathy with Horner syndrome is a Pancoast tumor until proven otherwise; a painless slowly progressive one after breast cancer treatment is radiation

pitfalls: Cervical radiculopathy and brachial plexopathy overlap in symptoms; EMG of paraspinal muscles and sensory nerve action potentials (preserved in root lesions, lost in plexus lesions) separate them
